cta.p: Everything in these guides is stocked, embroiderable and priced for teams.

pages.cardTitle: Choosing polos for a team uniform
pages.cardBlurb: Fabric weight, piqué vs jersey, colours that survive the wash — the five decisions behind a polo order that lasts.
pages.h1: Choosing polos for a team uniform.
pages.metaTitle: Choosing Team Polo Shirts: The Buying Guide | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: How to buy polos for a team — fabric weights and blends, piqué vs jersey, colour fastness, embroidery placement and the sizing spread that stops the second order going wrong.
pages.lede: The polo is the workhorse of team uniform — smart enough for customers, tough enough for the van. The difference between an order that looks sharp in month six and one that bags, fades and pills is five decisions made before you buy.

blocks.h2: Fabric first — weight and blend do the work
blocks.html:
Weight: workwear polos live around 180–220 gsm. Lighter feels flimsy and goes translucent in pale colours; heavier drinks money and dries slowly on the airer. Blend: poly-cotton (the classic 65/35) survives industrial washing and holds colour; cotton-rich feels nicer against skin but fades and shrinks faster; polyester-heavy wicks best for active roles at the cost of a synthetic hand-feel.

Knit: piqué — the textured waffle knit — is the uniform default: it holds its shape, hides minor wear, and takes embroidery beautifully. Smooth jersey reads more casual and shows embroidery pucker sooner. For teams, piqué wins on longevity almost every time.

blocks.h2: The five decisions in one table
head: Decision
Team default
Watch for
rows: Cotton-rich if comfort outranks wash life
Jersey for a softer, casual read
Pale colours show every mark by 10am
Cheap collars curl — the giveaway of a budget polo

blocks.h2: Branding and sizing — where reorders go wrong
blocks.html:
Embroider, don't print, for chest logos on kit that's washed weekly — the comparison explains why — and keep the logo left-chest, 8–10 cm wide, clear of the placket. Sizing spread: order against real people, not a guess at averages, and buy one spare set per size band — teams change faster than uniform budgets renew. And check the maker offers a consistent colour across sizes and reorders; a subtly different navy on the new starter's polo undoes the uniform effect the order paid for.

Long-sleeve variants, ladies' cuts and hi-vis-adjacent colours all exist across the polo range — spec them at order time, not as an afterthought.

faq.q: What weight polo shirt is best for work?
faq.a: 180–220 gsm is the workwear window — substantial enough to keep shape and stay opaque, light enough to wear year-round and dry overnight. Below about 170 gsm, pale colours go translucent and the polo reads as promotional rather than uniform.

faq.q: What's the difference between piqué and jersey polos?
faq.a: Piqué is the textured knit — it holds structure, hides wear and takes embroidery cleanly, which makes it the uniform default. Jersey is smooth and softer but shows pucker around stitching and reads more casual.

faq.q: How many polos does each team member need?
faq.a: Three to five each depending on wash frequency — enough that a mid-week disaster doesn't put a stained polo in front of a customer. Order a spare set per size band; new starters never arrive in convenient sizes.

pages.h1: Work trousers: cargo, holster or stretch.
pages.metaTitle: Work Trousers Guide: Cargo, Holster & Stretch | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: How to choose work trousers — cargo vs holster vs stretch-slim, knee-pad pockets and EN 14404, fabric weights, triple stitching and the details that survive a trade year.
pages.lede: Trousers take more punishment than any other garment on this site — kneeling, crouching, loaded pockets, constant abrasion. The style names (cargo, holster, stretch) describe real differences in how they carry weight and survive the year.

blocks.h2: Knee-pad pockets are a certification, not a gimmick
blocks.html:
Trousers with knee-pad pockets pair with foam inserts under EN 14404 — the knee-protection standard, certified as trousers-plus-pads together. For kneeling trades (flooring, tiling, joinery, groundworks) this is the single highest-value feature on the garment: the knees are the career-length decision. Two details matter at order time: top-loading pockets hold pads in place better through a working day, and pads are consumables — order spares with the trousers.

Fabric and construction carry the rest: 240–300+ gsm poly-cotton or ripstop for trade wear, triple-stitched seams at the seat and inside leg, and bar-tacks at pocket corners. Lighter stretch fabrics are genuinely better for active fitting work — but check the weight; slim cuts sold on comfort can be summer-weight cloth wearing trade styling.

items.l: Trade trousers should come in real leg lengths — hemming ruins cargo proportions
Loaded trousers need wide loops and a real belt — or braces buttons
Site trousers get filthy; check the label takes a hot wash before buying a fleet

blocks.html: Oil, paint and the stains that survive: getting grease out. The trouser range itself: shop trousers.

faq.q: What's the difference between cargo and holster trousers?
faq.a: Cargo trousers carry volume in fixed thigh pockets; holster trousers hang external pockets you can load with fixings and tools for fast access — a joiner's and electrician's favourite. Holsters win for speed, cargos for bulk, and many trades run both by task.

The knee-protection standard — certified as a system of trousers plus foam knee-pad inserts. If your work involves kneeling, trousers with certified pad pockets (and pads actually in them) are the highest-value feature you can buy.

faq.q: Are stretch work trousers durable enough for site?
faq.a: Good ones are — elastane-blend ripstops at proper weights handle site work while following the knee. The check is fabric weight: some slim styles are summer-weight cloth with trade styling. For heavy trades, look at 260 gsm upward or reinforced panels.

pages.cardBlurb: The layer that does the real winter work — synthetic vs merino, fit rules, and why cotton is banned from the list.
pages.h1: Base layers: the cheapest warmth you can buy.
pages.metaTitle: Thermals & Base Layers for Work: Buying Guide | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: How base layers actually keep outdoor workers warm — synthetic vs merino, the snug-fit rule, cotton's ban, and matching the layer to site work, cold stores and winter driving.
pages.lede: Crews spend hundreds on jackets and pounds on base layers — backwards, since the layer against your skin decides whether sweat becomes warmth or chill. It's the highest warmth-per-pound purchase in workwear, if you follow three rules.

blocks.html:
A working body sweats even in January. Whatever sits against the skin either moves that moisture outward — keeping the insulating layers dry and working — or holds it, and wet fabric conducts heat away many times faster than dry. That's the entire base-layer job, and it's why cotton is banned from this list: it absorbs sweat, stays wet, and turns into a refrigeration layer at the first tea break. The classic cotton tee under a site jacket is the most common self-inflicted cold on British sites.

Fit is function: a base layer wicks by touching skin — snug through the torso and arms, not compression-tight, never baggy. If it hangs loose it's just a thin shirt.

head: Synthetic (polyester/polypropylene)
Merino wool
rows: Slower to dry, warm even damp
Multi-day wear, moderate output, sensitive skin
No — synthetics melt. FR-rated or natural layers only
Acceptable where FR base layers aren't mandated — check policy

blocks.h2: Matching the layer to the work
blocks.html: Outdoor trades: lightweight synthetic top and leggings under normal workwear — warmth without bulk under the site layering system. Cold stores: the base layer is load-bearing kit under an EN 342 suit — wicking matters more there than anywhere, because sweat inside a freezer suit is the classic failure. Drivers and yard staff: a mid-weight zip-neck covers the in-and-out pattern without overheating the cab. Anyone in FR: the melt-layer rule owns the decision — FR-rated or natural fibre only, T-shirt included.

faq.q: Why is cotton bad as a base layer?
faq.a: Cotton absorbs sweat and holds it against the skin, and wet fabric strips body heat many times faster than dry. A cotton tee under winter kit becomes a chilling layer by the first break — synthetic or merino wicking layers exist to prevent exactly that.

faq.q: Should a base layer be tight?
faq.a: Snug — in contact with skin through the torso and arms so it can wick — but not compression-tight. Baggy defeats the mechanism entirely; it's just a thin shirt with an insulating air gap it can't use.

faq.q: Are merino base layers worth it for work?
faq.a: For multi-day wear, moderate work rates and anyone bothered by synthetic odour, yes — merino stays wearable for days and insulates even damp. For daily-washed fleets doing sweaty work, synthetics wick faster, survive hot washing and cost half as much.

pages.cardBlurb: Past the green labels: recycled fabrics, the durability argument, and the questions that separate substance from marketing.
pages.h1: Sustainable workwear, past the green labels.
pages.metaTitle: Sustainable Workwear: An Honest Buying Guide | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: What sustainable workwear genuinely means — recycled polyester and organic cotton, why durability is the biggest lever, end-of-life reality, and the greenwash questions to ask.
pages.lede: Workwear has a genuine sustainability story and a lot of green paint. The genuine part: garments bought once, worn for years and kept in service beat almost any fabric claim. Here's how to buy it with a straight face.

blocks.html:
The most sustainable garment in your fleet is the one that doesn't get replaced this year. A heavier, better-constructed polo that survives three years of washing outperforms a recycled-fabric one binned in twelve months — on carbon, water and waste. So the hierarchy runs: buy durable → keep it in service (care and repair-adjacent maintenance) → then let fabric claims break ties.

On those claims: recycled polyester (rPET) is the workhorse — bottle-derived fibre with genuinely lower impact than virgin, now common in fleeces, polos and softshells at trade prices. Organic and better-cotton programmes cut pesticide and water impact on the cotton share of blends. Both are real; neither makes a flimsy garment sustainable.

blocks.h2: Three questions that separate substance from paint
head: Ask
A good answer sounds like
A red flag sounds like
rows: What exactly is recycled, and how much?
GRS / OCS / OEKO-TEX named on the spec sheet
A green leaf on the swing tag and nothing else
A wash-count or wear-life the maker will state

blocks.h2: What a sustainable uniform programme actually does
blocks.html: Beyond the garments: rationalise the wardrobe (fewer, better lines beat a sprawling catalogue of cheap ones), embroider rather than print where possible so garments outlive design tweaks, rotate and launder properly so kit reaches its design life — most of the care hub is quietly a sustainability page — and plan end-of-life: de-branding and textile recycling for retired uniform rather than the skip. None of it is glamorous; all of it beats a leaf on a label.

items.l: A number and a scheme (GRS, OCS) — not an adjective
Durability someone will put in writing
Replaceable pads, buttons, zips — designed to be kept, not binned

faq.q: Is recycled polyester workwear actually better?
faq.a: Genuinely lower-impact than virgin polyester, yes — and now available at trade prices in fleeces, polos and shells. But the bigger lever is service life: a durable garment kept in use for years beats a short-lived recycled one on every environmental measure.

faq.q: What certifications should sustainable workwear have?
faq.a: Look for named schemes with numbers attached: GRS (Global Recycled Standard) or OCS for recycled content, OEKO-TEX for chemical safety, organic certification on cotton claims. An unquantified 'eco' label with no scheme behind it is marketing.

faq.q: What happens to old branded workwear?
faq.a: The responsible route is de-branding (unpicking or covering logos) and textile recycling or reuse schemes rather than landfill — some suppliers and laundries run take-back programmes. Planning it at purchase time beats improvising at skip time.

pages.cardBlurb: The under-served corner of workwear — what exists, what adapts, and what employers owe pregnant staff on fit and PPE.
pages.metaTitle: Maternity Workwear Guide: What Exists & What Adapts | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Maternity workwear options by trimester and role — purpose-made ranges, adaptable sizing, maternity hi-vis, and the employer's duty to provide PPE that actually fits.
pages.lede: Workwear catalogues mostly pretend pregnancy doesn't happen — and pregnant workers end up in wrong-sized men's kit that fits nowhere and protects worse. Better options exist; here's the honest map of them.

heroMeta.l: An employer duty, not a favour

blocks.html:
The strongest purpose-made maternity ranges cluster where the most pregnant workers are: healthcare tunics and scrubs with expansion panels and adjustable sides, maternity work trousers and leggings with over-bump or under-bump waistbands, and — genuinely — maternity hi-vis: certified vests and jackets cut for a bump, because a standard vest riding open at the front loses its certified visible area exactly where drivers look. Office-adjacent uniform (shirts, dresses) borrows well from mainstream maternity wear with an embroidered layer over the top.

Where purpose-made runs out, adaptation beats up-sizing: buying a men's XXL just makes everything long and loose in the wrong places while staying tight in the one place that matters. Adjustable-waist designs, wrap styles, stretch fabrics and layering pieces (open softshells, cardigans in uniform colours) carry the middle months better.

What works

rows: The best-served category — order early, sizes run out

Maternity hi-vis jacket, standard helmet & footwear

blocks.html: The employer side is a duty, not a perk. UK employers must risk-assess work for new and expectant mothers, and PPE law requires equipment that fits the wearer — a vest that gapes open over a bump or boots that no longer fit swollen feet fail that test. Uniform and PPE reviews belong in the pregnancy risk assessment alongside task changes, and reassessment each trimester is the practical rhythm.

faq.a: Yes — certified maternity hi-vis vests and jackets cut to stay closed over a bump, keeping the fluorescent area intact where a standard vest would gape open. For pregnant staff around vehicles, it's the correct answer rather than a bigger standard vest.

faq.q: Do employers have to provide maternity workwear?
faq.a: Employers must risk-assess work for new and expectant mothers, and PPE they provide must fit the wearer — which in practice means providing suitable maternity alternatives where standard kit no longer fits or protects. Uniform policy should follow the risk assessment.

faq.q: Can you just buy bigger sizes instead of maternity workwear?
faq.a: It rarely works — up-sizing adds length and shoulder width while staying wrong at the bump, and on PPE it can genuinely reduce protection (gaping hi-vis, trip-length trousers). Purpose-made or genuinely adjustable designs fit better and protect properly.

pages.cardBlurb: Nitrile vs vinyl vs latex, FFP grades at a glance, and the stock-room habits that stop single-use kit going to waste.
pages.metaTitle: Disposable PPE Buying Guide: Gloves, Masks & More | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Buying disposable PPE well — nitrile vs vinyl vs latex gloves, FFP mask grades, aprons and coveralls, sizing across a workforce, and storage that protects shelf life.
pages.lede: Single-use PPE is bought by the box and judged by the pallet — where small per-unit decisions multiply by thousands. The three that matter: the right glove polymer, the right mask grade, and a stock room that doesn't quietly ruin both.

head: Nitrile
Vinyl
Latex
rows: The problem — latex allergy is why many sites ban it
Only where policy allows and touch matters

blocks.klabel: The rest of the box wall
blocks.html:
Masks: the FFP grade question is settled in the EN 149 guide — buy the grade to the dust, remember NR means single shift, and remember fit testing for anything relied on at work. Aprons: polythene for food and care tasks, heavier PVC where splash is sustained. Coveralls: Type 5/6 disposables cover dusty and splash-adjacent one-offs — size up, since they tear at the crotch and shoulders when worn tight over clothing. Hairnets, beard covers, overshoes: hygiene-zone staples bought on fit and dispenser-friendliness more than anything.

Sizing across a workforce: gloves in S–XL with the split learned from the first month's usage (a 1:2:2:1 ratio is a common starting spread), and dispensers stocked per zone so the right size is the near size.

blocks.h2: Three habits that protect the pallet

items.l: Disposables have shelf lives — nitrile hardens, elastic dies; rotate stock
UV and heat age polymers in months — the window sill kills gloves
If a reusable would beat it, the comparison guide does that maths

blocks.html: Whether single-use is even the right format for a task: disposable vs reusable PPE settles it honestly.

faq.q: Are nitrile or vinyl gloves better?
faq.a: Nitrile for almost all working use — stronger, more puncture- and chemical-resistant, low allergy risk. Vinyl's place is brief, light, low-risk tasks where its lower price outweighs its fragility. Latex feels good but allergy risk has many workplaces banning it outright.

Yes — polymers age. Nitrile stiffens and loses elasticity, typically over a few years and much faster in heat and UV. Store boxes cool, dark and dry, rotate first-in-first-out, and treat brittle or discoloured gloves as expired.

faq.q: What sizes of disposable gloves should we stock?
faq.a: A spread from S to XL, weighted to your workforce — a 1:2:2:1 starting ratio is common, then adjust from real usage. Fit matters even on disposables: baggy gloves wreck dexterity and tight ones tear on donning.
